 Malaysia’s Biggest Banks to Lead Open Finance Rollout in 2028
 The rules extend to more banks and eligible e-money issuers in 2029, with mandatory sharing of small business data for qualifying providers in 2030. Fintech News Malaysia November 17, 2026 3 Mins Read

 Malaysia’s largest banks must be ready to share individual customers’ account data with their consent by 1 January 2028 under the open finance policy issued by Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM).
 The policy took effect on 17 November 2026, with mandatory data sharing set to roll out in stages.
 Customers will be able to view accounts they hold with different providers in one place or let a provider retrieve information directly instead of uploading documents.
 The data will go through the Open Finance Malaysia platform, run by Payments Network Malaysia (PayNet).
 BNM illustrates how open finance could simplify account viewing, credit assessments and document submission. 
 The mandate expands in three phases
 Licensed banks and Islamic banks with more than one million active individual and SME customers combined will be the first required to share individual customers’ data.
 The rules cover current balances and the past 12 months of transactions for deposit accounts, e-money accounts, credit cards and charge cards, where applicable.
 By 1 January 2029, the sharing requirement will extend to licensed banks and Islamic banks with more than 250,000 active individual and SME customers combined, as well as eligible e-money issuers with more than five million active users.
 Banks and e-money issuers covered by the mandate must also be ready to retrieve data at a customer’s request by that date.
 Prescribed development financial institutions with more than 250,000 active individual and SME customers combined must start sharing and retrieving data by 1 January 2030.
 The same deadline applies to SME account data for providers covered by the mandate with more than 30,000 active SME customers or users.
 BNM sets out what account and transaction data qualifying providers must share with customer consent and when. 
 Investment banks, insurers and takaful operators are not required to take part.
 Providers below the participation thresholds can join voluntarily if they meet the applicable rules.
 Customers can manage consent through a dashboard
 Customers must actively opt in to share their data. Providers cannot use pre-ticked boxes or bundle consent with unrelated terms.
 The dashboard lets customers check what they agreed to share, why and for how long, and withdraw permission.
 Permission for one-time access ends once the provider retrieves the data. Recurring access lasts up to six months at a time and requires renewal to continue.
 If consent expires or the customer withdraws it, providers must stop sharing and accessing the data under open finance.
 The provider that received the data must dispose of it unless it needs to keep or process it to meet legal or regulatory requirements.
 Providers must also have a plan for data breaches and work together when a complaint involves more than one provider.
 Each is liable for what it does or fails to do within its control.
